messages.subject: Re: moderation simple advice please
messages.subject_clean: moderation simple advice please
messages.body_plain:
It depends of what is your C moderator.
- If it is a grouping variable: multiple group model, and do group comparisons for the parameters of interest
- if the moderator is another factor measure by indicators: use the indProd function from semTools to define the indicators for the interaction factor, and the use probe2WayMC (also from semTools) to model the respective interaction

You can look at the help page of those functions to find simple examples
?indProd
?probe2WayMC

messages.body_plain:
Terrence, I expect you are correct, because AICc is known to be undefined in multivariate models (and many models used in biology are multivariate). Dave Anderson (of Burnham and Anderson) has claimed in his "little book" that AICc is useful for multivariate models even though it is not proper.

As a result of the influence of B&A in biology, biologists commonly use AICc in SEM studies and the AICcModavg package creates model comparison tables based on AICc using lavaan model objects. For this reason alone I would be very curious to see how it performs relative to AIC and CAIC in manifest (path) models like those studied in Lin et al., as well as in CFA models like Bollen et al. examined.

messages.subject_clean: Unbiased SRMR and confidence interval
messages.body_plain:
> When I use lavResiduals I get the unbiased SRMR (or CRMR, etc.) and SE but not the Z-test or p-value.

It's easy enough to add it to the data.frame in the $summary part of the output.

HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '
fit <- cfa(HS.model, data = HolzingerSwineford1939)
R <- lavResiduals(fit)
R$summary$usrmr.z <- R$summary$usrmr / R$summary$usrmr.se
R$summary$usrmr.pvalue <- 2*pnorm(-R$summary$usrmr.z)
R

> Is there a way to customize the function so that I get the test info for the unbiased estimate rather than only the biased sample SRMR?

You could wrap it up in a function.

myResids <- function(object) {
  R <- lavResiduals(object)
  R$summary$usrmr.z <- R$summary$usrmr / R$summary$usrmr.se
  R$summary$usrmr.pvalue <- 2*pnorm(-R$summary$usrmr.z)
  R
}

myResids(fit)

messages.subject: endogenous moderation
messages.subject_clean: endogenous moderation
messages.body_plain:
In the following well-fitted model, "M2" is acting as a moderator on the "M1 -> y" path (see also attached conceptual diagram):

df$M1_M2 <- df$M1 * df$M2
require(lavaan)

med.model <- '
M1  ~ a1*X1 + a2*X3 + a3*X4

messages.subject: Re: endogenous moderation
messages.subject_clean: endogenous moderation
messages.body_plain:
> However, since "M2" is an endogenous (measured) variable - and I know that e.g. the process macro only permits of exogenous moderators - I wanted to hear whether the experts of this group see any conceptual obstacles to this model?

The PROCESS macro does not use latent variable models.  I think moderators can be exogeonous, but try asking on SEMNET:

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?SUBED1=semnet&A=1

The issue to be wary of is that you need to treat your product term as exogenous, even if one (or in this case, both) of the variables in the product term is (are) endogenous.  So also correlate M1_M2 with the Xs (your syntax also omits the correlation of X1-3 with X4).  See models 3-5 in Figure 2:

https://doi.org/10.1080/00273170701341316

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.body_plain:
> repeat the name of the single indicator twice:

That is not necessary, and simply creates an extra copy of the same product term.  The point of the match=FALSE argument is that it will create all possible product terms.  Using the help-page data:

head(indProd(attitude, var1 = 1:2, var2 = 4, match = FALSE))
head(indProd(attitude, var1 = 1:2, var2 = c(4, 4), match = FALSE)) # extra variables

Robert, your Code B is wrong because those are not the variable names (the syntax thinks you are using the * operator to label a parameter).
Your Code A is wrong because you are putting a space in the variable names of the product terms (after the period), so the syntax doesn't find a variable named "Q35_1.", then furthermore must reach an error because there is no operator between that name and "Q61_1".

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

Hi everyone,

I am assessing moral violation ratings of adolescents. I am wondering how to interpret MIMIC models where I regress the factor onto sex, age, and political ideology. For sex and political ideology, I am using dummy codes. For age, I am not.

My data is coming from 11 different schools, so I am regressing the factor on 10 dummy coded school variables to control for school. Is it accurate to say I am controlling for these variables when I regress the factor on them?

Let's take the "loyalty" factor as an example. For this, I also regressed the political ideology identifier on two indicators because they involve a "US General" and an "American" as the protagonist, so I hypothesized that these might exhibit metric non-invariance for liberal vs. conservative students (they are also the items that show up has having correlated error variance in the modification indices).

Here is the syntax for the loyalty factor analysis:

loya <- '
loya =~ Q1_6 + Q2_6 + Q3_6 + Q4_6 + Q5_7 + Q6_7
loya ~ schooldummy_1
loya ~ schooldummy_10

loya ~ schooldummy_6

Q2_6 ~ libdem
Q6_7 ~ libdem
'

summary(loya1, fit.measures = TRUE, rsquare=TRUE, standardized = TRUE)
modificationindices(loya1, standardized = TRUE,sort. = TRUE)

When I run this code, I get the output provided below.

Here are my questions regarding interpreting this:

1. I can say I am controlling for school, sex, age, and political ideology by including these regressions, correct?
2. There is a significant (p<.05) difference in factor means for schools 10, 4, 6, 8, and 9. Is that correct?
3. There is a significant difference in factor means for age, sex, and being politically conservative (consrep) but not liberal (libdem), correct?
4. There is a significant direct effect of being conservative (consrep) on the Q2_6 and Q6_7 indicators, but only a significant direct effect on the Q6_7 indicator for liberals, correct?
5. The direct effects on the indicators (Q2_6 and Q6_7) are evidence of metric non-invariance?

Any additional thoughts/guidance anyone has is highly appreciated. I am using Brown's book, but would love to hear of additional resources.

Thanks so much,

Every path in an SEM is a slope.  The interpretations are the same as in any other regression model. So yes, if you have multiple predictors, your interpretation of a slope is always the expected change in the outcome given any other predictors of that outcome.

messages.subject_clean: good fit indices, but high SRMR in CFA
messages.body_plain:
> SRMR on .098. Do you have any idea why the SRMR is so large?

For local indicators of misfit (i.e., specific aspects of the data that your model fails to adequately reproduce), use the lavResiduals() function.  The SRMR is just the average of standardized residuals, so it is not very informative about why your model has mediocre fit.  It is almost 0.1, so on average, your model predicts correlations to be about 0.1 different than they actually are.  But there could be many small differences and either a few large ones or only 1-2 very large ones.  That is why you want to look at the actual standardized residuals (for a similar reason you would be curious about pairwise comparisons following a significant omnibus F statistic in ANOVA).

> And is this a good model fit?

That is not a question with a single answer.  In what ways does your model fit adequately, and in what was does it fit poorly?  Different indices express model fit in different ways, exposing different aspects of model misfit.  Here's a link to a recent SEMNET post wherein Keith provided a nice analogy.

https://listserv.ua.edu/cgi-bin/wa?A2=ind1912&L=SEMNET&X=B0001CD004E91656E2&P=79123

messages.subject: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I am an applied researcher, and I have a small question about test statistics especially b, standard errors & z-values that lavaan produces if a researcher is interested in testing mediation. My understanding is that, the product of two paths in a simple mediated relationship does not follow a normal distribution (according to recent publications of Andrew F. Hayes) and that the only way to tell if a mediated relationship is significant or not is by using confidence intervals. However, I am wondering lavaan does produce these statistics and I don't know if they are reliable or not (I guess they are reliable but I am a little confused). A clarification would be highly appreciated.

Thanks,

Pita
messages.body_snippet:

messages.subject: Re: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
messages.subject_clean: Test statistics in mediated relationships in lavaan
messages.body_plain:
Pita

You are correct, it cannot be assumed that the a*b term is normally distributed, but this is not new, there is a lot of literature about it.

Now, in lavaan if you do the analysis with the default features, this would lead to what is called the sobel test. Which means that the inference is made with the wald test assuming the product term is normally distributed.

There are mainly 2 ways that are recommended to deal with this, (a) use bootstrap Confidence Intervals and standard errors as bootstrap does not assume the parameter is normally distributed, for example

mod_med <- '
shs ~ cp*ple + b*grat
grat ~ a*ple

## indirect
ind := a*b
tot := a*b + cp ## total
'

fit_med_boot <- sem(mod_med, data=dat, meanstructure=T,fixed.x=F,
                    se="bootstrap", bootstrap=5000, verbose=T)
summary(fit_med_boot, standardize=T, rsquare=T)
parameterestimates(fit_med_boot, boot.ci.type="bca.simple",
                   level=0.95, standardize=T,
                   zstat = F, pvalue = F)

the second option (b) is to use the montecarlo simulation approach which is available with a function from semTools, like this

exp_ind <- 'a*b'
exp_tot <- 'a*b + cp'

mont_ind <- monteCarloMed(exp_ind, object = fit_med_sobel,
                          plot=T, CI=95)
mont_ind

mont_tot <- monteCarloMed(exp_tot, object = fit_med_sobel,
                          plot=T, CI=95)
mont_tot

messages.subject: Multilevel vs single level analysis convergence and interpretation
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel vs single level analysis convergence and interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,
I have a dataset with multiple responses per participant for each variable, so am modelling it with multilevel path analysis with clusters for each participant.
For one analysis, I am only interested in between-person effects, so I included my hypothesized model at level 2 and a saturated model at level 1. However, when I do this the model does not converge.

I also tried to run the analysis as a single level model where the data is each person's average response for each variable (i.e. one datapoint per person). This converged.

I assumed these two models were conceptually the same, so is it ok to just interpret the second model? And is there an intuitive reason why the second one converges but the first doesn't?

Thanks!

messages.subject: Re: invariance output interpretation
messages.subject_clean: invariance output interpretation
messages.body_plain:
you can tell that you have metric equivalence because the change in chisq relative to the change in df has a p >.05. This tells you that fixing the metric loadings of factors to items to be equal between groups causes very little change in the fit of the model to the data. The test for equivalent intercepts shows that the fit changes by much more than would be expected by chance. Even the change in CFI is much larger than the recommended .01 for this equivalence. So you have equivalent loadings but not intercepts. In a repeated measures study where the 2 groups are the same people at 2 times, this would be enough to allow comparison of group means. However, in a cross-sectional study, these 2 groups differ at their intercept or starting points by more than chance. Investigating which items have different intercepts becomes the question of interest. Are you able to speculate as to the cause of the difference--in what way are the 2 groups different? This suggests your groups do NOT come from the same population.
you can read a helpful tutorial on this matter in:
Brown, G. T. L., Harris, L. R., O'Quin, C., & Lane, K. E. (2017). Using multi-group confirmatory factor analysis to evaluate cross-cultural research: Identifying and understanding non-invariance. International Journal of Research & Method in Education, 40(1), 66-90. doi:doi:10.1080/1743727X.2015.1070823

messages.body_plain:
> Sobel test has suffered and probably succumbed to a lot of criticisms.

FYI, lavaan does not provide the Sobel test.  The Sobel test assumes that a and b have uncorrelated sampling distributions.  lavaan uses the delta method, which takes that correlation into account.  So it will work better than the Sobel test regardless, and the delta method yields nominal Type I error rates in sufficiently large samples.  The Monte Carlo method Mauricio mentioned is much less computationally intensive and works about as well as bootstrapping in smaller samples (but both break in small samples, for different reasons).

messages.subject: Re: Multilevel vs single level analysis convergence and interpretation
messages.subject_clean: Multilevel vs single level analysis convergence and interpretation
messages.body_plain:
> I assumed these two models were conceptually the same,

They are, conceptually.

> so is it ok to just interpret the second model?

The problem is that observed cluster means (subject means, in your case) are just estimates of the true population means.  Using observed sample statistics as proxies for unknown population parameters will generally lead to problems.  Here is some reading on the issue:

https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012869
https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024376

> And is there an intuitive reason why the second one converges but the first doesn't?

More complex model, requires more data for empirical identification.  How many clusters (people) do you have?  Here's some recent evidence that < 100 clusters is often doomed to failure, even if the model converges:

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1534205

> if I am only interested in within-person effects, is a single level model run on participant-centered data equivalent to level 1 of a multilevel model with clusters for each participant, with a saturated level 2 model?

No, the observations within each subject are still correlated (not independent data), so you would still at least need cluster-robust SEs.

Also, same issue as above: conceptually equivalent, but the problem is relying on sample-based means to center person-level data instead of estimating a model that takes their uncertainty into account.

> When I test this on my data, the regression coefficients and p values are the same to the first 2 decimal places, the covariances are a bit different but pretty close

Violated assumptions are a matter of degree, like any other effect size.  The worse the violation, the larger the differences.  If your results are similar, maybe your ICCs are not large, and your N is sufficiently large that the sample subject-means are good estimates of Level-2 intercepts.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

That is a very large model for only N=100 observations to handle.  Your model is identified in theory, but without sufficient data to estimate the parameters, it has an empirical identification problem.  This would be even more of a problem if your indicators are categorical, but even with continuous data, this is too large a model for such a small sample.

You could try using the parcelAllocation() function in the semTools package to reduce your model size to 3 items per indicator.  See the examples on the help page about saving the random allocations and using runMI() to account for the uncertainty of randomly assigning items to arbitrary parcels.

Thanks a lot! That is helpful and I will definitely look into those readings!

On Friday, January 17, 2020 at 5:30:10 AM UTC-5, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I assumed these two models were conceptually the same,
>
> They are, conceptually.
>
> > so is it ok to just interpret the second model?
> The problem is that observed cluster means (subject means, in your case) are just estimates of the true population means.  Using observed sample statistics as proxies for unknown population parameters will generally lead to problems.  Here is some reading on the issue:
>
> https://doi.org/10.1037/a0012869
> https://doi.org/10.1037/a0024376
> > And is there an intuitive reason why the second one converges but the first doesn't?
> More complex model, requires more data for empirical identification.  How many clusters (people) do you have?  Here's some recent evidence that < 100 clusters is often doomed to failure, even if the model converges:
>
> https://doi.org/10.1080/10705511.2018.1534205
>
> > if I am only interested in within-person effects, is a single level model run on participant-centered data equivalent to level 1 of a multilevel model with clusters for each participant, with a saturated level 2 model?
>
> No, the observations within each subject are still correlated (not independent data), so you would still at least need cluster-robust SEs.
>
> Also, same issue as above: conceptually equivalent, but the problem is relying on sample-based means to center person-level data instead of estimating a model that takes their uncertainty into account.
>
> > When I test this on my data, the regression coefficients and p values are the same to the first 2 decimal places, the covariances are a bit different but pretty close
>
> Violated assumptions are a matter of degree, like any other effect size.  The worse the violation, the larger the differences.  If your results are similar, maybe your ICCs are not large, and your N is sufficiently large that the sample subject-means are good estimates of Level-2 intercepts.
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

miFIT = runMI(model, ...)

produces standardized coefficients, but no their standard errors.

fit = sem(model, ...)

produces standardized regression coefficients but returns NA for the standard error and CIs.

Can standardizedSolution also calculate se/CIs for multiply imputed data sets, or is my best bet to calculate them for each individual data set and then pool them myself?

Best, Guido

messages.body_plain:
> I asked because I wanted to make a plot with standardized effects and CIs.

Oh ... well, that's actually a really good idea.  Preacher and Kelley recently advocated reporting CIs around effect-size estimates, and I agree with their reasoning (similar motivation, I'm sure, to your wanting error bars in your graph).  Even when the defined effect sizes might be of questionable value, I agree it is important to quantify uncertainty about the estimate.

For the record, I am not against providing a standardizedSolution.mi().  I just haven't been motivated to prioritize it above adding/maintaining other functionality in semTools.  My lack of motivation came not only from finding their use for hypothesis-testing dubious, but also from not finding a simple way to access lavaan's internal procedure for obtaining SEs of standardized estimates.  Perhaps I can ask Yves to make something available via the vcov(...) method.  I will make a note to post here if I find an easy enough solution to add this to semTools this summer (I doubt I will have time to program before that).

> I searched for Rubin's rule and found that there is a version for SEs, which I might use to estimate the pooled SEs myself.

See the final ?runMI help-page example to see how you can use the FUN= argument to store standardizedSolution() output for each imputation, which you could then use to pool SEs yourself.  Note that a pooled standardized estimate (i.e., the mean standardized parameter across imputations) will not be the same as the standardized pooled estimate (i.e., standardize the mean of unstandardized estimates across imputations, using model-implied SDs that are based on pooled parameter estimates).  But they will probably be close enough for graphing purposes.

data(datCat)
set.seed(123)
for (i in 1:8) datCat[sample(1:nrow(datCat), size = .1*nrow(datCat)), i] <- NA

catout <- cfa.mi(' f =~ 1*u1 + 1*u2 + 1*u3 + 1*u4 ', data = datCat,
                 m = 3, seed = 456,
                 miArgs = list(ords = paste0("u", 1:8), noms = "g"),
                 FUN = function(fit) list(STD = lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit)))
## custom function to extract estimate and SE from each imputation
getSTDs <- function(STD, lhs, op, rhs, group = NULL, level = NULL, COL = "est.std") {
    ROW <- STD$lhs == lhs & STD$op == op & STD$rhs == rhs
    if (!is.null(group)) ROW <- ROW & STD$group == group
    if (!is.null(level)) ROW <- ROW & STD$level == level
    STD[ROW, COL]
}
est <- mapply(getSTDs, STD = lapply(catout@funList, "[[", i = "STD"),
              lhs = "f", op = "=~", rhs = "u2")
SE <- mapply(getSTDs, STD = lapply(catout@funList, "[[", i = "STD"),
              lhs = "f", op = "=~", rhs = "u2", COL = "se")
mean(est) # pooled point estimate
sqrt(mean(SE^2) + (1 + 1/length(est))*var(est)) # pooled SE

You could wrap up that procedure in another function to vectorize over the estimates you want.

> On the other hand, I have not read any book on SEMs. Do you remember a justification for the recommendation you describe above?

Probably because historically, it took a while for software to implement correct SEs for standardized estimates.  But maybe also because that practice would be consistent with any other NHST context (e.g., Cohen's d is an effect-size supplement to a t statistic for NHST; you would not report separate t tests for raw data and z scores, although they would be identical in that context).  There is also the issue of whether the standardized parameter you estimate generalizes beyond the specifics of your design (e.g., if you sampled from a different (sub)population, the SDs of your variables could differ, making standardized parameters incomparable across contexts even in the population), which makes me uncomfortable with the knee-jerk automatic reporting of canned estimates of "standardized" effect size.  I recognize that SEMs often involve data with arbitrary scales (not just for latent variables), but I don't think dividing by sample SDs resolves that issue.

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

library(blavaan)

# The Holzinger and Swineford (1939) example
HS.model <- ' visual  =~ x1 + x2 + x3
              textual =~ x4 + x5 + x6
              speed   =~ x7 + x8 + x9 '

fit <- bcfa(HS.model, data=HolzingerSwineford1939)
summary(fit)

std_by <- standardizedposterior(fit)

apply(std_by, 2, mean) ### standardized posterior mean

> Thanks for your thoughtful response Terrence!
>
> It seems that you might have thought I wanted CIs to make inference. That was not the motivation. I like to report effect sizes that are intuitively accessible, which led me to standardized effects, and I like to report uncertainty, which led me to CIs.
>
> I hadn't thought about the difference between pooled standardized estimate and the standardized pooled estimates. What I am using are pooled standardized estimates, which seems intuitively right to me, because I want the CIs to reflect the uncertainty of the parameter estimate and the uncertainty introduced by missing data/imputation.
>
> The `FUN=` option is very useful, I hadn't seen that.
>
> It is a good point that generalization of standardized coefficients beyond the sample is unclear if a new sample has different data (variances). Currently I still prefer to report/plot standardized effects, because I hope this helps moving the readers attention away from NHST.*
>
> cheers, guido
>
> If I had the time, I'd implement a Bayesian model.
>
> On Monday, January 20, 2020 at 5:34:38 PM UTC+1, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > > I asked because I wanted to make a plot with standardized effects and CIs.
> >
> > Oh ... well, that's actually a really good idea.  Preacher and Kelley recently advocated reporting CIs around effect-size estimates, and I agree with their reasoning (similar motivation, I'm sure, to your wanting error bars in your graph).  Even when the defined effect sizes might be of questionable value, I agree it is important to quantify uncertainty about the estimate.
> >
> > For the record, I am not against providing a standardizedSolution.mi().  I just haven't been motivated to prioritize it above adding/maintaining other functionality in semTools.  My lack of motivation came not only from finding their use for hypothesis-testing dubious, but also from not finding a simple way to access lavaan's internal procedure for obtaining SEs of standardized estimates.  Perhaps I can ask Yves to make something available via the vcov(...) method.  I will make a note to post here if I find an easy enough solution to add this to semTools this summer (I doubt I will have time to program before that).
> >
> >
> > > I searched for Rubin's rule and found that there is a version for SEs, which I might use to estimate the pooled SEs myself.
> >
> > See the final ?runMI help-page example to see how you can use the FUN= argument to store standardizedSolution() output for each imputation, which you could then use to pool SEs yourself.  Note that a pooled standardized estimate (i.e., the mean standardized parameter across imputations) will not be the same as the standardized pooled estimate (i.e., standardize the mean of unstandardized estimates across imputations, using model-implied SDs that are based on pooled parameter estimates).  But they will probably be close enough for graphing purposes.
> >
> > data(datCat)
> > set.seed(123)
> > for (i in 1:8) datCat[sample(1:nrow(datCat), size = .1*nrow(datCat)), i] <- NA
> >
> > catout <- cfa.mi(' f =~ 1*u1 + 1*u2 + 1*u3 + 1*u4 ', data = datCat,
> >                  m = 3, seed = 456,
> >                  miArgs = list(ords = paste0("u", 1:8), noms = "g"),
> >                  FUN = function(fit) list(STD = lavaan::standardizedSolution(fit)))
> > ## custom function to extract estimate and SE from each imputation
> > getSTDs <- function(STD, lhs, op, rhs, group = NULL, level = NULL, COL = "est.std") {
> >     ROW <- STD$lhs == lhs & STD$op == op & STD$rhs == rhs
> >     if (!is.null(group)) ROW <- ROW & STD$group == group
> >     if (!is.null(level)) ROW <- ROW & STD$level == level
> >     STD[ROW, COL]
> > }
> > est <- mapply(getSTDs, STD = lapply(catout@funList, "[[", i = "STD"),
> >               lhs = "f", op = "=~", rhs = "u2")
> > SE <- mapply(getSTDs, STD = lapply(catout@funList, "[[", i = "STD"),
> >               lhs = "f", op = "=~", rhs = "u2", COL = "se")
> > mean(est) # pooled point estimate
> > sqrt(mean(SE^2) + (1 + 1/length(est))*var(est)) # pooled SE
> >
> > You could wrap up that procedure in another function to vectorize over the estimates you want.
> >
> >
> >
> > > On the other hand, I have not read any book on SEMs. Do you remember a justification for the recommendation you describe above?
> >
> > Probably because historically, it took a while for software to implement correct SEs for standardized estimates.  But maybe also because that practice would be consistent with any other NHST context (e.g., Cohen's d is an effect-size supplement to a t statistic for NHST; you would not report separate t tests for raw data and z scores, although they would be identical in that context).  There is also the issue of whether the standardized parameter you estimate generalizes beyond the specifics of your design (e.g., if you sampled from a different (sub)population, the SDs of your variables could differ, making standardized parameters incomparable across contexts even in the population), which makes me uncomfortable with the knee-jerk automatic reporting of canned estimates of "standardized" effect size.  I recognize that SEMs often involve data with arbitrary scales (not just for latent variables), but I don't think dividing by sample SDs resolves that issue.

messages.body_plain:
Brandon--
     You need to read Wu and Estabrook (2016) and decide for yourself. Yes, DF for these two models are equal. In the absence of equal thresholds, lavaan imposes other constraints to make the model identified. When thresholds are constrained equal, lavaan does not impose those additional constraints. Wu and Estabrook basically argue that "thresholds equal" *is* the configural or baseline equality model for measurement invariance with ordinal observed variables. The paper is heavy going, but only because you leave the domain of simple answers to face the actual complexity.
https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11336-016-9506-0
     Also, Terry has said he is working on a tutorial to help people dealing with the complexities of ordinal variable SEM. I'm sure ot will be awesome when available (probably should be a "Tutorial" paper in Psych Methods).
--Ed Rigdon

Hi,

I'm again having trouble with standardized estimates. This one is really peculiar, though, as it only occurs for one specific latent factor.

My model looks like this:

model <- "
D =~ d1 + d2 + d3 + ... + d36
H =~ h1 + h2r + h3 + ... + h32

P =~ p1 + p2 + p3 + ... + p9
G =~ g1

P ~ D + H
G ~ D + H
D ~~ HH
"

I then estimate the model via

model.fit  <- cfa(model,
                  data = data.model,
                  missing = "fiml",
                  std.lv = TRUE)

summary(model.fit,
        fit.measures = TRUE,
        standardized = TRUE,
        rsquare = TRUE)

messages.subject: Re: Error in Analysis of indirect and total effects (Error in parse(file = "", text = BODY.txt) : <text>:62:1: unexpected 'in')
messages.subject_clean: Error in Analysis of indirect and total effects (Error in parse(file = "", text = BODY.txt) : <text>:62:1: unexpected 'in')
messages.body_plain:
OK, this was a funny one.  One of your indirect effects was called "in" (product of paths i and n).  "in" is a reserved word in R:

?reserved

It is used to define the vector over which to loop (e.g., for (i in 1:3) {...}).  Any syntax will fail if you try to name something "in", but the error is much more informative if that thing is a variable instead of a parameter:

Data$in <- Data$HSR
model1 <- ' in ~ CWP '
fit1 <- sem(model1,data=Data, fixed.x=FALSE)
model1 <- ' HSR ~ in*CWP '
fit1 <- sem(model1,data=Data, fixed.x=FALSE)

Error in lavParseModelString(model) :
  lavaan ERROR: left hand side (lhs) of this formula:
    in ~ CWP
    contains either a reserved word (in R) or an illegal character: “in”
    see ?reserved for a list of reserved words in R
    please use a variable name that is not a reserved word in R
    and use only characters, digits, or the dot symbol.

I reported it on GitHub, so hopefully the next version of lavaan will print a more informative error message like the one above.

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/issues/170

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.subject_clean: Metric non-invariance, what's next?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Mauricio, I came back to reanalyze some more data, and this time I can't get the chi-square to change in my fit.metric by changing parameters like we did in the other model.

Here I am trying to test metric invariance for 4 groups at once.

Based on results form lavTestScore, I am trying to free the loading of the Q5_2 indicator in group 3. To do that I used this syntax:

cpa <- '
cpa =~ c(l1,l1,l1,l1)*Q1_2 + c(l2,l2,l2,l2)*Q1_8 + c(l31,l31,l31,l31)*Q2_2 +
c(l4,l4,l4,l4)*Q3_2 + c(l51,l51,l51,l51)*Q4_2 + c(l61,l61,l62,l61)*Q5_2

cpa ~~ c(1,1,NA,1)*cpa
'

No matter what parameters I try and free, e.g., L61, L62), I keep getting the exact same chi-square change indicating metric non-invariance (25.905, p=.039).

Here is the code I'm using to rerun the analysis after trying to free the parameters as above:

syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data=mft_dat, parameterization="theta",
                               ID.fac="auto.fix.first", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4))
cat(as.character(syntax.config))
summary(syntax.config)
## threshold invariance
syntax.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "auto.fix.first", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds")
## notice that constraining 4 thresholds allows intercepts and residual
## variances to be freely estimated in all but the first group & occasion
cat(as.character(syntax.thresh))
## print a summary of model features
summary(syntax.thresh)
## Fit a model to the data either in a subsequent step:
mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## or in a single step:
fit.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                            parameterization = "theta",
                            ID.fac = "auto.fix.first", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                            group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds", return.fit = TRUE)
## compare their fit to test threshold invariance
anova(fit.config, fit.thresh)

######
# METRIC INVARIANCE TESTING
######

## metric invariance
syntax.metric <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "auto.fix.first", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                               group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"))
summary(syntax.metric)                    # summarize model features
mod.metric <- as.character(syntax.metric) # save as text
cat(mod.metric)                           # print/view lavaan syntax
## fit model to data
fit.metric <- cfa(mod.metric, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## test equivalence of loadings, given equivalence of thresholds
anova(fit.thresh, fit.metric)

######
# SCALAR INVARIANCE TESTING
######

## scalar invariance
syntax.scalar <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",
                               ID.fac = "auto.fix.first", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                               group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings",
                                               "intercepts"))
summary(syntax.scalar)                    # summarize model features
mod.scalar <- as.character(syntax.scalar) # save as text
cat(mod.scalar)                           # print/view lavaan syntax
## fit model to data
fit.scalar <- cfa(mod.scalar, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## test equivalence of intercepts, given equal thresholds & loadings
anova(fit.metric, fit.scalar)

######
# INVARIANCE TESTING TABLE
######

## For a single table with all results, you can pass the models to
## summarize to the compareFit() function
compareFit(fit.config, fit.thresh, fit.metric, fit.scalar)

lavInspect(fit.metric, "cov.lv <http://cov.lv>")

messages.body_plain:
Lisa,
  Another thing you might consider is to estimate the model using both methods as a form of sensitivity analysis.  It may be that the degree of bias is small enough that you can still draw useful conclusions even if you cannot estimate the parameters without bias.  Estimation is not my area of expertise.  However, I recall Ronald Fisher pointing out that if the sample mean is an unbiased estimate of the population mean then the squared sample mean is a biased estimate of the squared population mean, which he took to suggest that bias need not be fatal to an estimation procedure.  (You could argue that Bayesian methods accept bias in exchange for precision.)  Often times in scale construction it is useful to test coarse hypotheses about parameters or an overall structure even if we cannot estimate individual parameters with great accuracy or precision.  For example, you might be able to distinguish well functioning from poorly functioning items even if your estimates are biased to some degree and too imprecise to reliably rank the items.  You could also use simsem() to simulate your model with your estimated parameters to evaluate the likely type and degree of bias under those conditions.  For instance, sometimes bias takes the form of bias toward or away from zero (rather than uniformly upward or downward) in which case estimates of zero population parameters may not be biased, possibly allowing you to distinguish zero from non-zero loadiings despite bias in the non-zero estimates.  It might be a good idea to compare your CFA item analysis results with classical item analysis to see if they lead to the same conclusions.  I am not encouraging small sample sizes, just thinking about what your study might be able to do despite the sample size if you cannot collect more data.

Good luck,
Keith

http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus

Hello,

regarding the question if level 2 needs to be populated:
Rosseel writes: "
Important notes

note that in level: 1 the colon follows the level keyword; if you type level 1:, you will get an error

you must specify a model for each level; the following syntax is not allowed and will produce an error:
    model <- '
        level: 1
            fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3
            fw ~ x1 + x2 + x3
        level: 2
    '

if you do not have a model in mind for level 2, you can specify a saturated level by adding all variances and covariances of the endogenous variables (here: y1, y2 and y3):
    model <- '
        level: 1
            fw =~ y1 + y2 + y3
            fw ~ x1 + x2 + x3
        level: 2
            y1 ~~ y1 + y2 + y3
            y2 ~~ y2 + y3
            y3 ~~ y3
"  (http://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/multilevel.html)

@Professor Jorgensen:
could you please further elaborate in regard to this statement?

Thank you,

Andreas

On Saturday, 2 November 2019 22:51:52 UTC+7, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > it seems to require that you have some variables included in level 2. However, my multilevel moderated mediation is all level 1 variables.
>
> Right, and all Level-1 variables have Level-2 components (the cluster means), so you need to model them.  If you have no hypotheses at Level 2, you can just omit the Level-2 model to obtain cluster-robust SEs and test statistics.
>
> If you do want to run a multilevel model, then your grouping variable needs to be a Level-2 variable, and you need to define a unique block of code for each level within each group:
>
> https://groups.google.com/d/msg/lavaan/fVWdx3b_q8o/7Bab6jXVDgAJ
>
> Terrence D. Jorgensen
> Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
> Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
> http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen
>

messages.body_plain:
I'm working on a mediation model that uses data from students in multiple courses. Each student is surveyed once, but there are 111 courses in the dataset, and I'd like to incorporate a random effect of course ID into my model. I've noticed that lots of the random intercept documentation online uses time series data (https://docplayer.net/21523270-Longitudinal-structural-equation-modeling.html), where the random intercepts are defined from factor levels where it looks like each level is its own column in the dataset.

I'm wondering if it's possible in lavaan to use random intercepts for purposes other than repeated measures? Or if it's feasible to use random intercepts when there are 111 levels of the factor?

Thanks for the help!

> Because the command above yields a probit threshold,  I am unsure whether I need to command lavaan to provide an intercept for the binary outcome variable (ideation~1)?
>
> I am confused about this because I notice that the model fit indices sometimes worsen when I include ideation~1  in the code. I also notice that when I have a saturated model, the df = -1. Does the code below automatically account one parameter pertaining to the probit threshold?

The model is not identified if you try to estimate both.  By default, it will estimate the threshold and fix the intercept to zero, whereas most GLM software (e.g., R's glm() function) does the opposite.   If you want to switch it around, you can estimate the intercept, but you would also have to fix the threshold to zero:

ideation | 0*t1

messages.body_plain:
> I would like to customize the confidence interval level (from 90% to 95%) for the model fit indices (e.g., RMSEA).

There is no argument to request a particular confidence level.  Are you aware that the 90% CI is customary because it is always used to test a one-tailed hypothesis?  Paying attention to one tail (e.g., the lower CI limit lets you test a H0 of not-close fit, the upper CI limit lets you test a H0 of close fit) thus always conforms to a one-directional 95% CI.

If you still want to customize your confidence level, you can see how to estimate the limits yourself using lavaan's source code:

https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_fit_measures.R#L820 (lower limit)
https://github.com/yrosseel/lavaan/blob/master/R/lav_fit_measures.R#L898 (upper limit)

The relevant code to extract is the lower.lambda() and upper.lambda() functions, which get passed to uniroot() to obtain the lambda values that are then plugged into the RMSEA equation in place of the F_ML.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

messages.subject_clean: Multilevel Moderated Mediation (1-1-1 with level 1 moderator)
messages.body_plain:
> could you please further elaborate in regard to this statement?

It means that if you do not specify a Level-2 model, you will only get cluster-robust SEs for your single-level model.  Perhaps that is all you want, but specifying a saturated model (i.e., freely estimate all Level-2 (co)variances).  If you hypothesize the same causal structure at both levels, you should specify the same model at both levels; then you could possibly test whether the paths are equivalent at both levels (which is unlikely) or calculate contextual effects.  Preacher and colleagues have written quite good articles explaining these issues in the context of multilevel mediation, most of which generalize to any SEM:

Hello all,

In his post <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/256053/variance-of-cohens-d-for-within-subjects-designs/258583#258583>, Mike Cheung <https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=kuTjTlsAAAAJ&hl=en> provides a lavaan solution to obtain SE for the effect size in pre-post experiment with one group of subjects.

But suppose we have two independent pre-post groups. I've calculated an effect size for the difference between two standardized pre-post differences of two independent groups of subjects. That is:

EFFECT SIZE = [Mean.difgroup 1/SD.difgroup 1] − [Mean.dif group 2 /SD.difgroup 2]

where Mean.dif is the difference between the means of pre- and post-tests of each group and SD.dif is the standard deviation of the difference scores for each of the two independent groups.
I was wondering how to obtain SE of this effect size via lavaan using Mike Cheung's approach <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/256053/variance-of-cohens-d-for-within-subjects-designs/258583#258583>?

messages.body_plain:
Internally standardizing (i.e., within each group separately) is problematic.  Suppose the pre-post difference is the same in both groups.  The group difference would be zero, and a standardized version of that effect (i.e., the group-by-time interaction) should also be zero.  But if group 1's SD.dif is smaller/larger than group 2's SD.dif, then the difference in (internally) standardized means would be nonzero.  Large differences in SD.dif between groups would make your effect appear large, even when there is no difference between groups.

The only way standardization works is to use a common norm. So you should probably pool SD.dif as well.  Using the principle behind the method Mike described, you would need to allow for group sizes to differ when you calculate SD.dif_pooled (e.g., see the formula for pooled "s" under Cohen's d: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Effect_size#Cohen's_d )

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam
http://www.uva.nl/profile/t.d.jorgensen

messages.subject: Re: Simulating Ordinal Data
messages.subject_clean: Simulating Ordinal Data
messages.body_plain:
Ilker,
  Here is a simple CFA example.

# Simulate ordinal data

require(lavaan)

# see ?model.syntax for details
simModel <- '
  factor =~ .8*item1 + .8*item2 + .8*item3 + .8*item4 # factor loadings
  item1 | -1*t1 + -.5*t2 + 0*t3 + .5*t4 + 1*t5 # thresholds
  item2 | -1*t1 + -.5*t2 + 0*t3 + .5*t4 + 1*t5
  item3 | -1*t1 + -.5*t2 + 0*t3 + .5*t4 + 1*t5
  item4 | -1*t1 + -.5*t2 + 0*t3 + .5*t4 + 1*t5
  factor ~ 0*1 # zero intercepts (not required)
  item1 ~ 0*1
  item2 ~ 0*1
  item3 ~ 0*1
  item4 ~ 0*1
  factor ~~ 1*factor # variances
  item1 ~~ 1*item1
  item2 ~~ 1*item2
  item3 ~~ 1*item3
  item4 ~~ 1*item4
' # end simModel

lavaanify(simModel)
ordinalData <- simulateData(simModel, sample.nobs=1000)
head(ordinalData, 10)
summary(ordinalData)

fitModel <- '
  factor =~ item1 + item2 + item3 + item4
  item1 | t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5
  item2 | t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5
  item3 | t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5
  item4 | t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5
  factor ~~ 1*factor
  item1 ~~ item1
  item2 ~~ item2
  item3 ~~ item3
  item4 ~~ item4
' # end fitModel

lavaanify(fitModel)
ordinalFit <- lavaan(model=fitModel, data=ordinalData)
summary(ordinalFit) # note unique variances rescaled

Keith
------------------------
Keith A. Markus
John Jay College of Criminal Justice, CUNY
http://jjcweb.jjay.cuny.edu/kmarkus
Frontiers of Test Validity Theory: Measurement, Causation and Meaning.
http://www.routledge.com/books/details/9781841692203/

messages.subject: Standard errors not computed with binary endogenous variable because the information matrix could not be inverted
messages.subject_clean: Standard errors not computed with binary endogenous variable because the information matrix could not be inverted
messages.body_plain:
I am new to lavaan and am trying to run a model for 2 binary outcomes with 2 continuous predictors. However, when I run it, it says: "Warning message:  In lav_model_vcov(lavmodel = lavmodel, lavsamplestats = lavsamplestats, :  lavaan WARNING: Could not compute standard errors! The information matrix could not be inverted. This may be a symptom that the model is not identified."

When I replace the binary outcomes with continuous outcomes, the model produces standard errors without a warning message. What am I doing wrong here?

Below is code to reproduce the error message. I would be extremely grateful for any help.

Many thanks,
Rose

library(MASS)
library(lavaan)

toy_data <- as.data.frame(mvrnorm(n=100,  mu = c(0,0,0,0), Sigma = diag(4)))

# Make new binary variables
toy_data$Y1 <- ifelse(toy_data$V1 > 0.5, 1, 0)
toy_data$Y2 <- ifelse(toy_data$V2 > 0.7, 1, 0)

# Rename continuous predictor variables as 'A' and 'B' for model
toy_data$A <- toy_data$V3
toy_data$B <- toy_data$V4

model1 <- '
# Regressions
Y1 ~ a1*A + b1*B #regression for Y1
Y2 ~ a2*A + b2*B #regression for Y2

# Variances and covariances
A~~va*A #variance in A
B~~vb*B #variance in B
Y1~~vy1*Y1 #variance in Y1
Y2~~vy2*Y2 #variance in Y2
A~~cvab*B #covariance between A and B
Y2~~cvy1y2*Y1 #covariance between Y1 and Y2
A~ia*1 #intercept for A
B~ib*1 #intercept for B
Y1~iy1(0.05)*1 #intercept for y1
Y2~iy2(0.17)*1 #intercept for y2

# Total effects
TotalY1:= a1 + b1
TotalY2:= a2 + b2'

Fit1 <- lavaan(model1, data=toy_data, ordered=c("Y1","Y2"), estimator = "WLSMV")
summary(Fit1)

### Re-run with continuous Y variables
toy_data$Y1 <- toy_data$V1
toy_data$Y2 <- toy_data$V2

Fit1 <- lavaan(model1, data=toy_data)
summary(Fit1)

messages.subject: Re: Defining items with cross loading in the model
messages.subject_clean: Defining items with cross loading in the model
messages.body_plain:
Your model is likely not statistically identified. You have few unique indicators (associated with only one common factor). In particular, factor B has no unique indicators, while A and C have only 1 unique indicator each. Indicators 4 and 6 load on THREE different common factors, which is rare in application. Generally, indicators loading on multiple factors this requires that factors be mutually orthogonal, and may also require starting values provided by the researcher. But you want to run a regression among these factors, so you can't make them orthogonal. If you want this to work, you will need other variables which distinguish the different common factors.

messages.body_plain:
I tried using the update() function but have the same problem. I assign cpa (now cpa_model) to model_fact at the top (model_fact <- cpa_model).

I ran the following syntax:

g1 <- "dissgroup"

mft_fact <- cpa_model

mft_dat <- cfs_middle

#Invariance testing

syntax.config <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data=mft_dat, parameterization="theta",

                               ID.fac="std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",
                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4))

cat(as.character(syntax.config))
summary(syntax.config)
## threshold invariance
syntax.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",

                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",

                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds")
## notice that constraining 4 thresholds allows intercepts and residual
## variances to be freely estimated in all but the first group & occasion
cat(as.character(syntax.thresh))

## print a summary of model features
summary(syntax.thresh)
## Fit a model to the data either in a subsequent step:
mod.config <- as.character(syntax.config)
fit.config <- cfa(mod.config, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## or in a single step:
fit.thresh <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                            parameterization = "theta",

                            ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",

                            group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4), group.equal = "thresholds", return.fit = TRUE)
## compare their fit to test threshold invariance
anova(fit.config, fit.thresh)

######
# METRIC INVARIANCE TESTING
######

## metric invariance
syntax.metric <- measEq.syntax(configural.model = mft_fact, data = mft_dat,
                               parameterization = "theta",

                               ID.fac = "std.lv <http://std.lv>", ID.cat = "Wu.Estabrook.2016",

                               group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                               group.equal = c("thresholds","loadings"))
summary(syntax.metric)                    # summarize model features
mod.metric <- as.character(syntax.metric) # save as text
cat(mod.metric)                           # print/view lavaan syntax

switched <- update(syntax.metric, change.syntax = "cpa ~~ c(1,NA,NA,NA)*cpa")
cat(as.character(switched))

cat(as.character(update(switched, change.syntax = "cpa =~ c(l61,l61,l62,l61)*Q5_2")))

## fit model to data
fit.metric <- cfa(mod.metric, data = mft_dat, group = g1, group.label=c(1,2,3,4),
                  parameterization = "theta")
## test equivalence of loadings, given equivalence of thresholds
anova(fit.thresh, fit.metric)

On Saturday, January 25, 2020 at 3:08:03 AM UTC-6, Terrence Jorgensen wrote:
> > I am trying to free the loading of the Q5_2 indicator in group 3. To do that I used this syntax:
>
> Nowhere in your syntax do you use the model "cpa <- ..." that you specified.  If you are relying on measEq.syntax() to write your syntax for you, it will always assume you are only providing a configural model (which is the name of the argument), so your labels will not be preserved.  You can only use the group.partial= argument to free a parameter in all groups/occasions.  If you want to free a parameter in only one group (or occasion), you can use the update() method to replace the specification of a particular parameter with your own custom syntax for that parameter (i.e., not the whole model, just 'cpa =~ c(l61,l61,l62,l61)*Q5_2').  See an example of this functionality at the bottom of this thread:  https://github.com/simsem/semTools/issues/60

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

I have question regarding the interpretation of path coefficients in a mediation model where the main predictor and mediator are continuous variables and the outcome variable is binary using probit link regressions.

Is probit link applied to all paths even when a path is between two continuous variables?

X --> M (path a1): this is a regression among two continuous variables (Does path a1 get tested with probit link or OLS?)
M--> Y (path b1): regression between a continuous variable and binary outcome (probit link)
X --> Y (path c): regression between a continuous variable and binary outcome (probit link)

Below is the command I used to run the model.

fit14a=lavaan(modmediation14a, data=data1, ordered=c('ideation'), estimator='DWLS', se = 'bootstrap', bootstrap=10000L,  link = "probit", fixed.x=FALSE, auto.var = TRUE, meanstructure=TRUE)

Thank you in advance for providing clarification.

Luis

On Sat, Jan 25, 2020 at 12:31 AM Terrence Jorgensen <tjorge...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Because the command above yields a probit threshold,  I am unsure whether I need to command lavaan to provide an intercept for the binary outcome variable (ideation~1)?
> >
> > I am confused about this because I notice that the model fit indices sometimes worsen when I include ideation~1  in the code. I also notice that when I have a saturated model, the df = -1. Does the code below automatically account one parameter pertaining to the probit threshold?
>
> The model is not identified if you try to estimate both.  By default, it will estimate the threshold and fix the intercept to zero, whereas most GLM software (e.g., R's glm() function) does the opposite.   If you want to switch it around, you can estimate the intercept, but you would also have to fix the threshold to zero:
>
> ideation | 0*t1
